title: Should @Transactional go on the class, the implementation, or the interface? Explain how JDK dynamic proxies differ from CGLIB proxies and why you should always put @Transactional on the implementation.
shortTitle: @Transactional on class vs interface — JDK proxy vs CGLIB

s1_definition.profdef: Spring applies `@Transactional` through an AOP proxy that wraps your bean and begins, commits, or rolls back the transaction around the method call. Spring can create two kinds of proxies: a JDK dynamic proxy, which implements the bean's interfaces and only sees annotations on interface methods, or a CGLIB proxy, which subclasses the concrete class and sees annotations on the class. Spring Boot defaults to CGLIB proxying since Spring 5.x. Because a CGLIB proxy subclasses the implementation and cannot reliably read interface-level annotations, you should always put `@Transactional` on the implementation class or its methods, not on the interface, so it works regardless of which proxy type is used.
s1_definition.analogy: Think of the proxy as a security guard standing in front of the real banking clerk. With a JDK proxy, the guard only reads the rulebook posted on the public counter (the interface) — if the "transaction required" rule is written there, he enforces it. With a CGLIB proxy, the guard is actually a stand-in wearing the clerk's uniform (a subclass), and he only reads the rules written in the clerk's own personal notebook (the implementation), not the public counter. Since Spring Boot hires the uniform-wearing stand-in by default, you must write the transaction rule in the clerk's own notebook — the implementation — or it gets ignored.
s1_definition.oneliner: Spring Boot uses CGLIB by default, which proxies the concrete class, so always annotate the implementation, not the interface, or `@Transactional` may be silently ignored.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Spring applies `@Transactional` through an AOP proxy that wraps your bean and begins, commits, or rolls back the transaction around the method call. Spring can create two kinds of proxies: a JDK dynamic proxy, which implements the bean's interfaces and only sees annotations on interface methods, or a CGLIB proxy, which subclasses the concrete class and sees annotations on the class. Spring Boot defaults to CGLIB proxying since Spring 5.x. Because a CGLIB proxy subclasses the implementation and cannot reliably read interface-level annotations, you should always put `@Transactional` on the implementation class or its methods, not on the interface, so it works regardless of which proxy type is used.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Think of the proxy as a security guard standing in front of the real banking clerk. With a JDK proxy, the guard only reads the rulebook posted on the public counter (the interface) — if the "transaction required" rule is written there, he enforces it. With a CGLIB proxy, the guard is actually a stand-in wearing the clerk's uniform (a subclass), and he only reads the rules written in the clerk's own personal notebook (the implementation), not the public counter. Since Spring Boot hires the uniform-wearing stand-in by default, you must write the transaction rule in the clerk's own notebook — the implementation — or it gets ignored.

**One line to remember:** Spring Boot uses CGLIB by default, which proxies the concrete class, so always annotate the implementation, not the interface, or `@Transactional` may be silently ignored.

sections.s2_technical:
Spring does not add transaction behavior to your bytecode directly. Instead it creates a proxy object that wraps your bean. When someone calls a method on the proxy, the proxy starts a transaction, calls the real method, and then commits or rolls back. This is why `@Transactional` only works on calls that come through the proxy from outside the bean.

There are two proxy mechanisms. A JDK dynamic proxy is created by the JDK's `java.lang.reflect.Proxy`. It works only if your bean implements at least one interface, because the proxy itself implements those same interfaces. A JDK proxy reads the transaction metadata from the interface methods it implements. A CGLIB proxy is created by generating a subclass of your concrete class at runtime and overriding its methods. It does not need an interface because it extends the class directly, and it reads the metadata from the concrete class.

Historically, Spring used JDK proxies when the bean had an interface and fell back to CGLIB only when there was no interface. But since Spring 5 and Spring Boot 2, the default changed: `@EnableTransactionManagement` and Spring Boot both default to `proxyTargetClass = true`, which means CGLIB is used even when interfaces are present. So in a modern Spring Boot app, your service is almost always wrapped by a CGLIB subclass proxy.

This is exactly why the placement of the annotation matters. A CGLIB proxy subclasses the implementation, so it reliably sees `@Transactional` on the implementation class and its methods. It does not reliably pick up annotations that exist only on the interface, because CGLIB is working at the class level, not the interface level. If you put `@Transactional` only on the interface and Spring uses CGLIB, the annotation can be silently ignored and your method runs with no transaction at all. That is a dangerous bug in a bank, because a transfer that should have been atomic might partially apply.

The safe and recommended practice is to always put `@Transactional` on the implementation. For example, define a plain interface `TransferService` with no transaction annotations, and put `@Transactional` on the implementation class `TransferServiceImpl` or on its methods. For example `public class TransferServiceImpl implements TransferService { @Transactional public void transfer(...) { ... } }`. This works under both JDK and CGLIB proxies, so it is robust no matter how Spring is configured.

There are a few more practical consequences of CGLIB. Because CGLIB creates a subclass, your class and the transactional methods cannot be `final`, and the class cannot be `final` either, since you cannot subclass or override final things. A `final` method simply will not be proxied, so its `@Transactional` is ignored. Also, CGLIB cannot proxy private methods, so `@Transactional` on a private method does nothing. And the self-invocation rule still applies: if a method inside the bean calls another method on `this`, the call does not go through the proxy, so the second method's `@Transactional` is ignored regardless of proxy type.

A senior-level summary is that the Spring Framework reference documentation itself recommends annotating concrete classes rather than interfaces, precisely because the choice of proxy strategy affects whether interface annotations are honored. Putting the annotation on the implementation removes all ambiguity. If you genuinely need interface-based JDK proxies, you can set `proxyTargetClass = false`, but even then annotating the implementation is the defensive choice.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — At the National Bank of India, a developer defined a `TransferService` interface and put `@Transactional` on the interface method, then wrote a `TransferServiceImpl` without the annotation. In testing, transfers that should have rolled back on failure instead left money half-moved. This is exactly the JDK-proxy-versus-CGLIB problem — because Spring Boot used CGLIB by default, the interface annotation was ignored and the method ran with no transaction.

Problem 2 — Another developer made a service method `final` for safety, and its `@Transactional` silently stopped working because CGLIB cannot override a final method. This is exactly why transactional classes and methods must not be final.

Problem 3 — The fix for both was moving the annotation to the implementation. This is exactly the recommended practice: annotate the concrete class so it works under any proxy type.

What the code will do. The `Account` class holds balance with debit and credit. A `TransferService` interface declares the transfer method with no annotations. A `TransferServiceImpl` puts `@Transactional` on its transfer method so both JDK and CGLIB proxies honor it. The demo simulates a CGLIB proxy wrapping the implementation, shows a successful transfer committing and a failing transfer rolling back, and contrasts what would happen if the annotation were only on the interface.

sections.s5_journey:
Input data: a successful transfer of Rs.50,000 from SAV2001 to CUR3001, then a failing transfer of Rs.9,999,999 that must roll back.

Step 1. The caller invokes transfer on the proxy, not on the real implementation. Because Spring Boot uses CGLIB, the proxy is a subclass of the implementation. It inspects the concrete class method and finds the Transactional annotation there. Since the annotation is on the implementation, it is honored.

Step 2. The proxy begins a transaction, then calls the real transfer method on the target. Rajesh has enough balance, so he is debited Rs.50,000 and Priya credited Rs.50,000.

Step 3. The real method returns normally. The proxy commits. Rajesh is now Rs.950,000 and Priya Rs.300,000.

Step 4. The caller invokes transfer again for Rs.9,999,999. The proxy begins a new transaction and calls the real method.

Step 5. Rajesh does not have Rs.9,999,999, so the real method throws. The proxy catches the exception, rolls back, and re-throws. Because of the rollback, nothing changed: Rajesh stays at Rs.950,000 and Priya at Rs.300,000. Had the annotation been only on the interface, CGLIB would not have seen it, no transaction would have started, and a partial debit could have leaked.

sections.s6_takeaway:
Spring does not weave transaction code into your bytecode directly. It wraps your bean in an AOP proxy that begins the transaction, calls your real method, and then commits or rolls back. There are two kinds of proxy. A JDK dynamic proxy implements your bean's interfaces and reads the Transactional annotation from the interface methods. A CGLIB proxy generates a subclass of your concrete class at runtime and reads the annotation from the class itself. Since Spring 5 and Spring Boot 2, the default is CGLIB, with proxyTargetClass set to true, even when your bean has an interface.

This default is exactly why annotation placement matters. A CGLIB proxy subclasses the implementation, so it reliably sees Transactional on the implementation class and its methods, but it does not reliably pick up an annotation that lives only on the interface. In my banking project a developer once put Transactional on the interface method and left the implementation bare. Because Spring Boot used CGLIB, the annotation was silently ignored, no transaction was ever started, and a failing transfer left money half-moved instead of rolling back. That is a serious bug in a bank.

The fix, and the practice I always follow, is to keep the interface clean and put Transactional on the implementation class or its methods. That works under both JDK and CGLIB proxies, so it is robust no matter how Spring is configured. The Spring reference documentation itself recommends annotating concrete classes rather than interfaces for exactly this reason.

There are a few related CGLIB rules I always keep in mind. Because CGLIB creates a subclass, the transactional class and its methods must not be final, since a final method cannot be overridden and its annotation will be ignored. CGLIB also cannot proxy private methods, so Transactional on a private method does nothing. And the self-invocation rule still applies under any proxy: if a method calls another annotated method on this, the call does not go through the proxy and the annotation is skipped. So my rule of thumb is simple: always annotate the implementation, keep transactional classes and methods non-final and public, and never rely on self-invocation for transactions.
